subject: Biology
title: Translation: Building Proteins
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Translation: Building Proteins.

hook.text: Ribosomes read mRNA three letters at a time. Each triplet, called a codon, codes for one amino acid.

buildup.text: Transfer RNA molecules bring the right amino acid to match each codon on the mRNA.

discovery.text: Amino acids link together in a chain that folds into a functional protein.

twist.text: A single mRNA can be read by many ribosomes at once, producing proteins in bulk.

climax.text: From insulin to collagen, every protein starts as a string of codons on mRNA.

punchline.text: Three letters at a time, proteins are born.

quiz.question: What is a codon?
options: A three-letter sequence coding for an amino acid

details.summary: Translation converts mRNA's nucleotide sequence into a chain of amino acids at the ribosome. Transfer RNA molecules deliver amino acids matching each three-letter codon, building the protein one amino acid at a time until a stop codon signals completion.
details.whyItMatters: Translation is where genetic information becomes functional protein. Understanding this process is essential for developing antibiotics that target bacterial ribosomes and for engineering proteins with new functions.
takeaways: Ribosomes read mRNA codons and coordinate amino acid assembly
Each tRNA carries a specific amino acid matching its anticodon to the mRNA codon
Translation proceeds from the start codon AUG to a stop codon

faq.question: How fast does translation occur?
faq.answer: Bacterial ribosomes add about 20 amino acids per second, while eukaryotic ribosomes are slightly slower at about 6 per second. Multiple ribosomes can translate the same mRNA simultaneously, producing many protein copies efficiently.

faq.question: Why do many antibiotics target translation?
faq.answer: Bacterial ribosomes differ structurally from human ribosomes, allowing drugs to block bacterial protein synthesis without harming human cells. Antibiotics like tetracycline and erythromycin exploit these differences to selectively kill bacteria.
